title: Your First Days Of School Classroom Management Checklist ement-checklist/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin describes the first days of school as a critical, fleeting window when students are open to new habits, and outlines a short checklist of 'framework' procedures teachers must teach first: classroom rules and consequences, restroom policy, entering and leaving the room, lining up and walking in line, giving attention on signal, sitting and listening during lessons, and raising hands. He argues these foundational routines set the tone for everything that follows, using a sloppy line as an example barometer of broader classroom habits. To teach them thoroughly, he recommends four strategies: explain why a procedure matters, model it in detail, let students practice before demanding perfection, and reteach immediately whenever standards slip. Used together, the checklist and the four teaching strategies are meant to preserve students' early-year eagerness and maturity throughout the rest of the school year.
points: Teach only a small set of foundational 'framework' procedures first, including rules, consequences, restroom policy, lining up, and raising hands.
Treat seemingly minor routines like walking in line as a barometer for the overall state of classroom management.
Use four teaching strategies for procedures: explain why, model in detail, let students practice, and reteach whenever standards slip.
Give students a chance to 'try it on' through practice before expecting perfection or even competence.
Reteach immediately if behavior drifts from expectations, since letting something slide signals that the original standard no longer applies.
quotes: You have a captive group of students, fresh and open to your way of doing things. But it won’t last.
Those important few form the basis, or framework, for successful classroom management. They prepare the way for all the other procedures, routines, and expectations to be taught.
A sloppy, distracted line means that more of the same shoddy habits and behaviors are happening, and will continue to happen, in the classroom.
Students are often resistant when asked to do something they don’t understand. “What’s the point?” is always rattling around in their heads. Explaining why cuts through this resistance.
Give students a chance to “try it on” before asking for perfection, or even competence. Let them practice.
If you let something–anything–go, you’re communicating to your students that what you originally told them, taught them, and asked of them, is no longer valid.
